title: Of woodlice and men: A Bayesian account of cognition, life and consciousness (with Karl Friston)

abstract: In this interview, Karl Friston discusses the origins and implications of the Free Energy Principle (FEP), from childhood observations of woodlice to a comprehensive framework for understanding cognition, life, and consciousness. Friston recounts how watching woodlice scurry in sunlight and slow in shade led to the insight that biological self-organization can be explained by simple thermodynamic principles. The conversation covers the FEP's relationship to Bayesian inference, predictive process

methods.name: Long-form Q&A interview of Karl Friston by Fortier and Friedman
methods.description: The work is a published interview (ALIUS Bulletin): Martin Fortier and Daniel A. Friedman pose long-form questions and Karl Friston answers them.
methods.evidence: An interview with Karl Friston By Martin Fortier & Daniel A. Friedman

methods.name: Interviewer-framed contrasts of Bayesian brain, predictive coding and FEP
methods.description: Questions set out formal Bayesian belief-updating equations and contrast the three frameworks before asking Friston to respond.
methods.evidence: Do you agree with this characterization of the Bayesian brain hypothesis, of predictive coding, and of the free energy principle?

methods.name: Questions drawing on empirical literatures (fluency, psychosis, altered states)
methods.description: Interviewers bring in specific prior work, e.g. Chetverikov's fluency/disfluency 'sweet spot' results and competing models of psychosis, as prompts.
methods.evidence: According to Chetverikov, at the experiential level human beings aim at finding a sweet spot between fluency and disfluency rather than minimizing disfluency.

key_findings: Friston recounts that the prototype of the FEP came from noticing, at age eight, that woodlice simply moved faster in the sun and slower in the shade.
Friston distinguishes the FEP as an unfalsifiable principle from process theories such as predictive coding, which are empirically testable hypotheses.
Friston argues the Bayesian brain and predictive coding lack the enactive aspect of the FEP because they do not consider entropy reduction.
Friston contends that apparent inverted-U 'sweet spots' are all explained by minimizing expected free energy, not by different laws at different levels.
Friston holds that consciousness is the process of inference, so any free-energy-minimizing system is conscious to some degree; self-awareness requires a self-other model.
key_findings_evidence: I realized their “scurrying” had no purpose or intent: they were simply moving faster in the sun—and slower in the shade.
On this view, the relation between the free energy principle and predictive coding is the relationship between a principle and a process theory.

It is this enactive, embodied, extended, embedded, and encultured aspect that is lacking from the Bayesian brain and predictive coding theories; precisely because they do not consider entropy reduction.
I see a singular and simple explanation for all the apparent dialectics above: they are all explained by minimization of expected free energy, expected surprise or uncertainty.
consciousness is a process and it is the process of inference. Therefore any system that minimizes variational free energy is conscious to a greater or lesser extent
